newsitem.title: UK: Dlr deflated in Europe by U.S./Japan rate rethink.
newsitem.headline: Dlr deflated in Europe by U.S./Japan rate rethink.

text.p: A wave of uncertainty about the prevailing outlook for U.S. and Japanese interest rates saw the dollar sink by more than two yen and more than 1-1/2 pfennigs in Europe on Friday.

While U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin helped stabilise the unit late in the session, by reasserting the appropriateness of his long-standing "strong dollar" policy, comments from Federal Reserve officials downplayed the chances of another imminent U.S. interest rate rise.
The trigger for today's dollar lurch came from Fed chairman Alan Greenspan, who talked of growth slowing later this year.

"The Greenspan speech was the trigger and it has shaken out a lot of people who were hoping to cruise into the weekend in fairly quiet market conditions," said Stewart Newnham, analyst at First Chicago in London.

Greenspan said overnight he expected economic growth to slow later this year and he saw scant signs now of a resurgence of inflation. Although the Fed chief said the central bank would have to act if growth didn't slow, the market took the comments to suggest there would be no interest rate rise at the next policy- making Open Market Committee meeting on May 20.

At 1530 GMT, the dollar was trading 120.70/80 yen compared with 123.70/80 late Thursday but off a two-month low at 120.40. Against the mark, it was at 1.6890/95 compared with 1.7071/76 late yesterday and just off a one-month low at 1.6855.

Traders said a series of stop-loss orders exaggerated the day's slide in thin markets and in the absence of any fresh economic news. Key chart supports were taken out and look like neutralising the longer-term dollar trend.
While the change in U.S. rate expectations softened the dollar across the board, dollar/yen was the driving force as talk of higher Japanese rates contrasted with the U.S. picture.

Another barrage of comments from Japanese ministry of finance officials warning against recent excessive yen weakness combined with speculation about a rise in Japanese interest rates this summer. A report in Japan's Nikkei Kinyu said talk of a rate rise in July was pushing government bond yields higher.

"The underlying focus is on Japan and what Japanese investors are doing with their capital," said one senior trader at a U.S. bank here. "There is concern that they are more withdrawn from global markets since the Golden Week holiday and this has acted as a drain on currencies that have been dependent on the Japanese search for yield," he said.
Unwinding of sterling/yen positions has been one feature of the week's activity as this had been one of the most attractive long-term yield plays for the Japanese.
As a result, sterling's slide too was precipitous again today, losing up to three pfennigs against the mark and bringing the loss this week alone to almost 10 pfennigs.

Sterling's close correlation with dollar/mark has been one factor behind its weakness, traders said. But this was exaggerated by growing expectations the new UK Labour government will be more likely to bring the pound into European monetary union in the years ahead and at a lower rate than at present.
The Swiss franc gained further, meantime, as the unwinding high-yield plays globally benefited the low-yielding currencies these plays had been funded in.

The prospect of a broad-based EMU, including the UK and Italy, also worried investors about the stability of the new euro and this has brought the Swiss franc's status as a low-inflation, safe-haven back into focus, analysts said.
